name: CLOVES syndrome
aliases: congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi and spinal/skeletal anomalies

reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: The acronym captures the core features: congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi, and spinal/skeletal or scoliosis anomalies
Characteristic truncal lipomatous masses are present from birth, often with overlying vascular staining and a wide sandal gap or large fatty overgrowth of the trunk
Combined capillary, venous, lymphatic, and sometimes arteriovenous malformations distinguish it from simpler overgrowth conditions
Part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS) caused by post-zygotic (mosaic) activating variants in PIK3CA
Because the variant is mosaic and post-zygotic it is not inherited and overgrowth is typically segmental and asymmetric, with severity depending on the tissues involved
Molecular diagnosis usually requires deep sequencing of affected tissue rather than blood, since the mosaic variant may be undetectable in leucocytes
Targeted PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibition has emerged as a therapeutic option for severe PROS, alongside multidisciplinary supportive and surgical care
reference.pathophysiology: CLOVES syndrome results from somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants in PIK3CA, which encodes the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase. Constitutive activation of PIK3CA drives the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promoting unregulated cell growth, proliferation, and survival in the tissues carrying the variant. Because the mutation arises after fertilisation, only a subset of cells is affected, producing the segmental, asymmetric overgrowth of fat, vessels, skin, and bone that defines the phenotype; the distribution and burden of mutant cells determine clinical severity.
additionalDifferentials: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome and other PIK3CA-related overgrowth phenotypes
additionalInvestigations: Deep or high-sensitivity sequencing of affected (lesional) tissue for mosaic PIK3CA variants
MRI of affected regions and the spine to map lipomatous overgrowth and vascular malformations
Vascular imaging to characterise capillary, venous, lymphatic, and arteriovenous components
Assessment for spinal and skeletal anomalies including scoliosis
Coagulation studies where extensive venous or lymphatic malformation raises thrombotic risk
Renal and abdominal imaging given the reported association with Wilms tumour in PROS
redFlags: Signs of high-flow arteriovenous malformation or thromboembolism from extensive vascular lesions
Rapidly progressive spinal or paraspinal overgrowth causing cord compression
New abdominal mass or haematuria prompting evaluation for Wilms tumour
Localised intravascular coagulopathy with bleeding or clotting complications
reference.prognosis: The course is highly variable and depends on the extent and location of overgrowth and vascular involvement; some individuals have limited disease while others face progressive functional and orthopaedic complications. Emerging targeted pathway inhibitors and multidisciplinary care have improved management of severe disease.
pitfalls: Testing blood rather than affected tissue and wrongly excluding a mosaic PIK3CA variant
Confusing CLOVES with Klippel-Trenaunay or Proteus syndrome despite differing genetics and complications
Underestimating thrombotic risk in extensive vascular malformations
Neglecting spinal surveillance for scoliosis or cord compromise
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
